Tax Credit Spillovers and Administrative Burden: Evidence from Hawaiʻi's EITC Expansion

Laura Kawano, University of Michigan

Dylan T. Moore, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa

Sisi Zhang, Hawaiʻi Department of Taxation

National Tax Association Annual Conference · November 2026

The views expressed here are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views or policies of the Hawaiʻi Department of Taxation.

Tax Credits Reach Only the Families Who File

▶

Many families do not claim benefits they are entitled to. A growing literature points to administrative burdens.

▶

For benefits delivered through the tax code, the burden is filing a return:

▶

Families must file a tax return to receive the credit.

▶

Low-income households may have no statutory obligation to file.

▶

These are often the very families the credits target.

How large is the gap in Hawaiʻi?

Among unmarried adults with income under $50K, an estimated 24–37% file no state return
(ACS-aligned, an upper bound).

At Low Incomes, Many Tax Units File No Return

Filing rate = resident returns ÷ ACS tax units

Below $50K, 24–37% of unmarried adults and 11–29% of married couples file no return (2017–2024, upper bounds).

2022 to 2023: the unmarried filing rate moves from 0.627 to 0.632. No visible aggregate response.

Notes: Resident returns (dependent filers excluded) ÷ ACS 1-year tax units, group quarters excluded. By income: each married-couple bin has under 100 ACS observations (hollow markers), so that line is noisy. *2020: experimental ACS weights. Upper bounds: military households and dependent young adults remain in the ACS base.

This Paper: Does Filing Respond to the Value of Filing?

▶

Setting. Hawaiʻi, tax year 2023: the state EITC doubles and becomes refundable, and the Food/Excise Tax Credit doubles.

▶

Data. Hawaiʻi resident income tax returns, 2017–2024, as cell-level refiling rates.

▶

Design. A triple difference in refiling across family type, base-year income and year, using the simulated change in state credits.

Preliminary findings

Refiling rises with the size of the credit change: 0.042 pp per $100 (SE 0.014),
about +0.21 pp at the average $508 change.

A placebo lead is near zero, and the second year looks like the first.

A small effect, and likely attenuated per dollar actually faced. The 2018 EITC introduction points the same way.

Why it matters for filing

A refundable EITC pays families with no state tax liability, but only if they file. The 2023 changes raised the return to filing most for working parents with low income.

FETC: a refundable credit of a fixed amount per exemption, meant to offset the general excise tax.

Notes: Refundability and permanence come from Act 114 (2022), effective tax year 2023. The 40% rate and the FETC increase come from Act 163 (2023) and are scheduled to sunset after tax year 2027. We refer to the combined 2023 change as Act 163.

The change

2018–22: a 20% match on the federal EITC, but nonrefundable, so it paid little at low incomes. The FETC added $110 per exemption.

2023: the match doubles to 40% and becomes refundable. The FETC doubles and reaches $60K.

The change peaks near $16.6K, at about $2,890 a year.

Notes: 2023 EITC is 40% of the federal credit (head of household); FETC for three exemptions. The simulated 2018–22 EITC may be understated where the nonrefundable cap binds; if so, the 2023 change shown is overstated there.

Design: A Triple Difference in Base-Year Income

ygkt = αgk + λkt + μgt + f(ΔBgkt) + εgkt

▶

y: refiling rate (pp) for family type g, base-year income bin k, year t.

▶

Income is fixed in the base year t − 1, before the reform can move it.

▶

ΔB: the simulated change in state EITC + FETC at that income for that family type (the curves just shown). f is linear, binned or a spline.

▶

Fixed effects: type × bin (α), bin × year (λ), type × year (μ).

▶

So f is identified only by three-way variation in ΔB: families whose incentive rose more against those whose incentive rose less or not at all.

Notes: 6 types × 20 bins ($5K, 2023 dollars) × 2018–2024, cells weighted equally. Standard errors clustered by type × bin (120 clusters).

Interpretation: A Reduced Form, Likely Attenuated

▶

ΔB is assigned at base-year income. The change a family actually faces depends on its income in year t.

▶

So the estimate is the reduced form of a simulated-instruments design. We do not observe the first stage.

▶

Incomes move: in high-ΔB cells some families rise into the phase-out, and in zero cells some fall into eligibility. If so, π < 1 and the effect per dollar actually faced is larger than our estimate.

D = πZ + v
E[y | Z] = (π β) Z

Z: assigned ΔB. D: change actually faced.
π: first-stage slope.

The dose itself

The simulated 2018–22 credit may be understated. If so, the assigned 2023 change is too large where the cap binds, which would also push the per-dollar estimate down.

A caveat

If families judge the incentive from last year's return, ΔB is the incentive they perceive and nothing is attenuated.

The fix

Estimate π by running observed income changes through the 2023 schedules.

Limits: What These Data Cannot Yet Show

Separate the EITC from the FETC

Entered separately: EITC +0.087 (0.020), FETC −0.31 (0.17). After the fixed effects the two changes correlate 0.60 and both come mostly from 2023.

Test the design with power

The zero-change tests never reject, but their 95% interval (−0.30 to +0.37 pp) is wide enough to hide a gap as large as Act 163's whole effect.

Weight, count and see entry

Every cell counts equally, without population weights, and refiling says nothing about people who never filed.

Rule out other 2023 changes

The same act expanded the dependent care credit, which also favors working parents. Other payments (federal CTC, rebates) show no effect of their own when added.

The slope is similar without 2020–22, with nominal income bins, and (less precisely) using only 2019 and 2023.

Conclusions: Filing Responds to Its Value, Modestly

▶

The 2023 changes raised the return to filing by up to about $3,000 for low-income parents, and far less for others at the same income.

▶

Holding base-year income fixed, refiling rises with the size of the credit change: about 0.04–0.06 pp per $100. A placebo lead is near zero and the second year looks like the first.

▶

These are reduced-form effects of assigned incentives. Per dollar actually faced, the effect is likely larger.

▶

The 2018 EITC introduction points the same way, on weaker evidence.

▶

Refiling is one margin. An estimated 24–37% of lower-income unmarried adults file no return, and ACS-based coverage is too noisy to show an effect of this size.

▶

Next: individual-level estimates, with counts, weights, entry by never-filers and the first stage.

Hawaiʻi Policy Background

▶

Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)

▶

Credit for low- and middle-income working families

▶

Phases in at low earnings, plateaus, then phases out

▶

Federal EITC since 1975; states followed from the 1980s. Hawaiʻi's EITC began in tax year 2018 (Act 107, 2017).

▶

Food and Excise Tax Credit (FETC)

▶

Refundable credit, created in 2008, to offset Hawaiʻi's general excise tax

▶

A fixed amount per qualified exemption, phased by federal AGI

Who Does Not File? Aligning Returns with the ACS

▶

Numerator: resident returns by federal AGI, dropping returns of filers claimed as dependents.

▶

Denominator: ACS 1-year tax units, 2017–2024, built to look like returns:

▶

married couples are one unit; every other adult is a unit; group quarters dropped;

▶

income moved toward federal AGI: SSI removed, only taxable Social Security kept.

▶

Coverage = returns ÷ ACS units by $5K bin; one minus coverage is the non-filing rate.

▶

Still an upper bound on non-filing: military households and young adults claimed as dependents remain in the ACS base.

Notes: Returns from the Department of Taxation; ACS from IPUMS USA. Single parents are not reported as a rate.

How Many Do Not File?

24–37%

of unmarried adults with income under $50K file no return

11–29%

of married couples with income under $50K

Who they are

Mostly childless adults with low income: 30–70% non-filing below $20K, in every year.

Zero income

About 55,000 unmarried ACS units against about 13,800 returns (2023).

State-only filers

3,700–4,600 returns a year at zero federal AGI file only to claim the refundable FETC.

Married parents

Look well covered: non-filing mostly 10–40% across income bins, no sign of over-coverage.

Does Coverage Respond? Not Detectably

▶

Same triple difference with returns ÷ ACS units as the outcome: 3 family types × 14 income bins, 2017–19 and 2022–24.

▶

Coverage elasticity with respect to the state credit: −0.04 (SE 0.08); 95% CI about −0.19 to +0.11.

▶

Cumulative curves for 2022→2023: between −0.05 and +0.04 over $10–55K, never beyond 0.92 SE.

What to make of it? Not much yet

The denominator may be wrong (military households, dependents, single parents misaligned with ACS units), and ACS cells are noisy. Refiling has a well-defined denominator: last year's filers.

Appendix: Hawaiʻi's EITC Schedule, 2022 and 2023

The rate doubles, from 20% to 40% of the federal credit.

For three or more children the maximum rises from about $1,400 to about $3,000.

From 2023 the credit is refundable, so it reaches families with little or no state tax.
